# The appointments Haniyasubime made — and who is keeping them

Take Haniyasubime's stories in sequence. They are not episodes; they are appointments — and the modern trades are keeping them.

## At a Glance

- **Temple:** Haniyasubime
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Domain of influence:** Clay, Pottery, Earth
- **Pattern seats:** 3
- **Sectors touched:** Energy & Natural World · Home & Lifestyle · Health & Wellbeing
- **Strongest seat:** Agriculture, Food & Harvest
- **Series:** The Resonance Files, No. 203 of 597

## The Cycle, Read Forward

### Agriculture, Food & Harvest — through *The Dying Goddess Bears the Clay Kami*

Izanami gave birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi, and the fire burned her so badly that she sickened and lay dying.  From her body in its extremity came the last kami of the living generation: from her vomit, the metal-mountain deities Kanayamahiko and Kanayamahime; from her urine, the water goddess Mizuha-no-me; and from her bowels, the brother and sister of clay — Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime (Kojiki, birth of Kagutsuchi; the Nihon Shoki gives her the parallel names Haniyama-hime, 'Clay-Mountain Princess,' and Haniyasu-no-kami).

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The clay-soil princess born from Izanami's dying body; the soil that bears the crop is hers.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. That is the cycle working: story becomes duty, duty becomes trade.

### Food & Hospitality — through *A Name That Means 'Clay That Yields'*

Hani-yasu is a name that explains itself, the way kami names so often do.  Hani (埴) is potter's clay, the earth dug from the subsoil that holds water and takes any shape; yasu (安/易) is 'easy, gentle, workable.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The clay-soil princess; every earthen vessel that holds the meal is her making.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. The trade thinks it is optimizing a process. It is re-enacting a charter.

### Yoga, Meditation & Holistic Wellness — through *Three Gifts of Civilization from One Body*

Read together, the kami born from Izanami's failing body form a complete inventory of material culture.  Kanayama-hime, from the vomit, is metal — ore, smelting, the smith's art.

The atlas states the seat in one line: *The clay-soil princess; earthen grounding and the patient calm of the potter's wheel.* The story above is the long version of the same sentence. Industries do not invent their archetypes; they inherit them and call them best practice.

## The Theme That Runs the Cycle

Haniyasubime's mythology is two sentences long in the Kojiki — and they are among the most striking in the whole canon. Everything else the tradition knows about her is in her name: hani, potter's clay, and yasu, the yielding. The potters of Japan's ancient kiln towns supplied the rest of her story — a thousand years of practice laid at her feet.

## The Method, Stated Plainly

None of this is numerology. A seat exists only where the match can be argued from the deity’s documented domains and deeds — weighted, published, and falsifiable. The derivation, the weights, and the challenge process are public on the [methodology page](/patterns/methodology/). If a seat in this file reads wrong, the atlas itself tells you how to prove it — and the correction becomes part of the record.

## For the Ones Who Work There

If you work in agriculture, food & harvest, food & hospitality, or any trade this temple holds a seat in, this is the honest version of what a placement means: your industry beside the story it has been re-telling all along — on the temple floor itself, before an audience that came specifically to read it. The [patron tier](/haniyasubime/patron/) and the [advertising terms](/terms/advertising/) describe the mechanics; the resonance above describes the fit.
